cards.text: Job, a man from Uz, has lost his children, his flocks and his health (Job 1:1, 13-19; 2:7). His friend Bildad the Shuhite just spent a whole speech on how the lamp of the wicked goes out (Job 18:5-6). Now Job answers, and I bet he's been holding this one in.

cards.question: Job asks his friends how long they'll keep tormenting him. What does he say they're crushing him with?

cards.text: Ten times now, Job says, they've reproached him. TEN. Friend, that's not a visit anymore. That's a subscription.

cards.question: Job says that even if he really has gone astray, his error concerns him alone.

cards.text: Then Job flips the script. If his friends want to rise above him and use his disgrace against him, they need to understand something first.

cards.question: Bildad talked about a net catching the wicked (Job 18:8). Job says a net has been drawn around him. Who does Job say drew it?

cards.text: Job says that when he cries out, 'Violence!' he gets no response. He calls for help, and there is no justice.

cards.question: Job pictures himself as a traveler who can't get anywhere. What does he say God has done to his way?

answers.text: Blocked it so he cannot pass
Washed it out with a flood

cards.text: Then the picture changes from a blocked road to a man who used to be honored, and Job says God has stripped him of his honor.

cards.question: Job says God stripped him of his honor. What does he say God removed from his head?
Job says God tears him down on every side until he is gone and uproots his ___ like a tree.

cards.text: Then it gets heavier. Job says God's anger burns against him.

cards.question: Job says God still counts him among His friends.

cards.text: Now Job talks like a town under attack. He says God's troops advance together and build a ramp against him.

cards.question: Job says God's troops build a ramp against him and camp around his ___.

cards.text: Job says God has removed his brothers from him and his acquaintances have abandoned him. Friend, even in the junk drawer the rubber bands said good morning.

cards.question: Job says his kinsmen and friends are still standing by him.
Even in his own house, Job says his guests and maidservants count him as a ___.
Job calls for his own servant and even pleads with him out loud. What does the servant do?

cards.text: It reaches all the way home. Job says his breath is repulsive to his wife, and he is loathsome to his own family.

cards.question: Job says even the people you'd least expect scorn him when he shows up. Who are they?
Job says those he loves have turned against him.

cards.text: Job says his skin and flesh cling to his bones, and then: 'I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.' Teeth don't even HAVE skin, friend. That's how close it was.

cards.question: Job turns to his friends and begs them twice for the same thing. What is it?
Job asks his friends why they persecute him the way God does.

cards.text: Then Job makes a wish. He wishes his words were recorded and inscribed in a book.

cards.question: Job wants his words to last, written with an iron stylus on lead or chiseled in ___ forever.
Then the whole speech turns. Right in the middle of all his pain, what does Job say he knows?

cards.text: Here it is in full: "But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth." Friend, set the dough down for a second and read that one again.

cards.question: Job says even after his ___ has been destroyed, yet in his flesh he will see ___.
Job says someone else will see God for him and tell him about it.

cards.text: Then Job says, "How my heart yearns within me!" Friend, I waited years in a dark drawer for one slice of light, so I get that one.
Last, Job turns to a warning. His friends might say, let's persecute him, since the root of the matter lies with him.

cards.question: Job warns the friends who keep putting the blame on him. What does he say they should fear for themselves?

cards.text: Job says wrath brings punishment by the sword, so they may know there is a judgment. And that's where Job leaves it for now, friend, but this conversation is far from over.

findings.problem: The card says Bildad 'spent a whole speech on how the lamp of the wicked goes out.' Only Job 18:5-6 is about the lamp. The rest of Job 18 covers traps, terrors, disease and the wicked man being forgotten. This makes the lamp image bigger than the text does, and it isn't one of Papa Dorin's jokes.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The setup 'a traveler who can't get anywhere' is a paraphrase of the right answer, 'Blocked it so he cannot pass.' It rules out the other two answers, so the baker doesn't have to think.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: No story card sets up verse 10. The fill in the blank asks the baker to supply the next word of the line ('uproots his ___ like a tree'). That tests wording the baker hasn't seen, not meaning they can reason out.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Card 14 frames Job 'like a town under attack,' which points the baker toward 'gate.' The text says 'tent.' Nothing in the setup lets the baker reason to 'tent,' so getting it right is luck, and the blank is guessing the next word of the line.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Most story cards in stop 1 (cards 5, 7, 9, 12 and 14) are plain restatements of the verse with no Papa Dorin voice. Card 3 has the stop's only laugh. Several moments, like Job flipping the friends' accusation back on them, could carry a respectful laugh without muddying a fact.

rule.text: Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it.

findings.problem: The joke 'Teeth don't even HAVE skin, friend. That's how close it was.' does two things. It plays on how odd the wording of Scripture's idiom is, and it gives the idiom a meaning ('how close it was'). The meaning of the phrase in Job 19:20 is debated, and idioms get their own pop-up.
findings.question: Can Papa Dorin joke about how odd a Bible idiom's literal wording is, or does that count as humor targeting Scripture? And can a story card state an idiom's meaning when the idiom pop-up already covers it?
